# Theoretical Foundations and Platform Specification

### Chapter 1: Architectural Theoretical Background
The historical contextualization of distributed computing architectures in modern enterprise environments necessitates an expansive review of organizational theory, socio-technical alignment, and legacy communication primitives. Throughout the preceding four decades, institutional methodologies governing software engineering evolved through distinct paradigmatic phases, ranging from early monolithic mainframe deployments to federated micro-architectures. Within this broader academic and philosophical framing, modern systems design reflects continuous trade-offs between centralized data governance and autonomous domain boundaries. Organizations routinely encounter coordination bottlenecks when decomposing bounded contexts, highlighting Conway's law across disparate engineering divisions. Each operational boundary introduces latent communication overhead, network partition susceptibility, and distributed consensus complexities. Consequently, infrastructure practitioners must exercise judicious architectural discipline when designing transactional workflows across multiple geographic availability regions. ## Concrete System Requirements
- Requirement 1: The user shall be able to log in using standard credentials.
- Requirement 2: The system shall display a list of account transactions.
